item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The hamster ball procedure is ingenious, and more importantly entertaining.
But more secure would be keeping it in one room strapped to a Roomba-like device programmed to frequently randomly change speed and direction. While keeping a safe distance from all walls.
Or, since it's hematite, float it in mid-air 2 meters from anything solid with magnets.

I can't quite wrap my head around how this would affect fluids. Drop it in a pool and…what? The water would become monstrously immobile so that it effectively acts as a solid? Or would Brownian motion and tiny eddies mean that no particular bit of water had a stable enough velocity from moment to moment to be affected? Or would it gradually reinforce all those tiny micro-motions, with the net effect being 1.6 cubic meters of water that maintains a constant temperature no matter how much heat the surrounding environment absorbs from it?

Edit: and I just realized, description doesn't say how big or heavy the thing itself is. We can extrapolate based on the 10cm platform that it is rather small, but seems a major oversight for what is supposed to be a technical write up.

item.title: Issues with the containment logic
item.content:encoded:
If the effect wears off slower than it builds up, then just switching storage location between just two locations back and forth will only slow down the build up of the effect on each location.

You need more than 2 locations; I'm not quite sure on the math to figure it out though. But unless the wearing off takes precisely the same amount of time as the build up, or the time it takes to transport is enough to make it reach zero; you'll need at least 3 locations.

Also, keeping it in place for long enough to produce the "unstoppable/unmovable" effect, might result in whatever it is affecting breaking off and floating towards the horizon due to the rotation of Earth (the centrifuge force would get stronger), or possibly in random directions due to the Orbit of the Earth around the Sun, or even worse, the Sun around the center of the galaxy. I'm not sure of the magnitude of the effect for the duration you described in the article though; but even if it's not too strong, it might still induce stresses on the building. Perhaps the containment procedures should be amended to mention it should be kept suspended on a net made of some very light material, at more than 1.6m away from anything other than the net itself; or if it's magnetic, using some form of magnetic levitation, and perhaps even in vacuum to avoid influencing the air?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This… needs to be kept in motion, constantly changing. Moving it in a circle constantly changes the angle of momentum, so inertial buildup shouldn't be a problem. It will NOT make a cyclone, momentum doesn't "circle".

Moving it every 30 days is… impossible. 30days*24hours*60minutes*60seconds/160 seconds.
Inertia will increase to a factor of 1.17^16,200

That ends up being 4.08*10^1104. More than 40,000 *((1 googol)^11) times it's normal inertia. You are NOT getting that started again.

Just put the platform moving in a small, slow circle, with the stone in a padded receptacle, and the backup room used in case something breaks. Possibly move it every 30 days anyway for maintenance.

item.title: Re: 17
item.content:encoded: Holy crap! That's a complete coincidence and I never intended it when I was writing the article, but now that I look back at it you're absolutely correct. Good catch! That makes for an interesting interpretation of 289, though. Perhaps it is not actively increasing inertia, just increasing the localized importance and occurrence of the number 17 and the inertia thing is a side effect of it locally messing up the physics formulas.

Has anyone else noticed the large amounts of the number 17? Site-17, 1983 (17 years before 2000, bit of a stretch), 17%, 17 minutes during the recover, item # 289 (17^2), and more I probably missed. Was this just a coincidence, or was it on purpose, and why?

item.title: A theoretical application for this SCP
item.content:encoded: Stated in this article, it says that something that maintains it's movement in the presence of SCP-289 for greater than 800 seconds will no longer be able to be stopped. Theoretically, this means that the device or being witnessing this is expressing a nearly unlimited amount of torque, so I suppose that you could write of a test where someone builds an "inertia generator", based on a gyroscope or other rotary implement that would work off the principle of this SCP. And even if it doesn't actually mean that the inertia is infinite, and eventually will slow down by experiencing force, simply re-exposing the mechanism to the SCP, could very well act as a way to recharge it. A vehicle with an inertial drive core and a specialty gearbox could be used as a new form of transport, or an electrical generator can have it's pinion engaged by an inertial core. The possibilities seem to be nearly endless in this way, and could very well be written about, and I feel that an SCP as interesting as this deserves that kind of depth. Thank you for giving me something so fun to think about!

item.title: Re: Storage concerns
item.content:encoded:
You're 100% correct on the storage precautions. I think I wrote this before the general consensus of "locked box" storage for Safe SCPs was decided on. I'll rework the first section in the near future.

As for the tether, my thinking was that as long as the helicpoter maintained a steady forward motion at the same speed, the inertial buildup would keep 289 fairly steady and bypass most of the sway. Landing could be tricky, but really all that would be necessary would be letting 289 impact a sturdy wall before landing the helicopter.

item.title: Storage concerns
item.content:encoded:
I know this discussion is 3 years old, but still. Given that this is classified as a Safe SCP, the level of precaution in storage and personnel assigned seems excessive. Also, does SCP-289 affect itself? I suppose not, in that it would have become completely unmovable itself after a long enough period.

And the tether it was attached to would have been affected by the SCP as well - although I suppose they could have stabilized it by keeping it steady before beginning transit, it seems more likely that the motion of the helicopter would cause it to swing, and then be continually affected by the SCP until the tether swung in an arc high enough to impact the helicopter rotors - sending the SCP flying off and away.

I am apparently in a very quibbling mood today.
